questions.question: Explain why factoring +b instead of −b from the pair −bx − by makes the grouping fail, and how the negative factor fixes it.
questions.expected_answer: Taking out +b leaves (−x − y), which cannot match the first pair's bracket (x + y), so no common bracket exists and the method stalls. Dividing by −b flips both signs inside, leaving (x + y) — dividing by a negative reverses signs — so the brackets match and the common bracket can be factored out.

questions.question: Describe what to do when the terms of a four-term expression refuse to group in their given order, and why this is allowed.
questions.expected_answer: Rearrange the terms so that terms sharing factors (kin) sit together — e.g. reunite the a-terms and the b-terms — then pair and group normally. Addition is commutative, so reordering terms changes nothing about the expression's value.

questions.question: In your own words, explain how the matching-brackets checkpoint works as a self-check, and what the final verification of a grouping answer looks like.
questions.expected_answer: The method only succeeds if both pairs, after factoring, contain the identical bracket; a mismatch flags an earlier error (usually a sign) before a wrong answer can be written. The final check is expansion: multiplying the two answer brackets must return all four original terms with their original signs.
